claim: Ion channel complexes promote action potential initiation at the mammalian axon initial segment (AIS).
source: Ion channel complexes promote action potential initiation at the mammalian axon initial segment (AIS), and modulation of AIS size by recruitment or loss of proteins can influence neuron excitability.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about AIS function.

claim: Modulation of AIS size by recruitment or loss of proteins can influence neuron excitability.
source: Ion channel complexes promote action potential initiation at the mammalian axon initial segment (AIS), and modulation of AIS size by recruitment or loss of proteins can influence neuron excitability.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Endocytosis contributes to AIS turnover.
source: Although endocytosis contributes to AIS turnover, how membrane proteins traffic to this proximal axonal domain is incompletely understood.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing from existing knowledge.

claim: How membrane proteins traffic to the AIS is incompletely understood.
source: Although endocytosis contributes to AIS turnover, how membrane proteins traffic to this proximal axonal domain is incompletely understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Neurofascin186 (Nfasc186) has an essential role in stabilising the AIS complex to the proximal axon.
source: Neurofascin186 (Nfasc186) has an essential role in stabilising the AIS complex to the proximal axon, and the AIS channel protein Kv7.3 regulates neuron excitability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: The AIS channel protein Kv7.3 regulates neuron excitability.
source: Neurofascin186 (Nfasc186) has an essential role in stabilising the AIS complex to the proximal axon, and the AIS channel protein Kv7.3 regulates neuron excitability.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about Kv7.3 function.

claim: Vesicles transport Nfasc186 to the soma and axon terminal where they fuse with the neuronal plasma membrane.
source: Vesicles transport Nfasc186 to the soma and axon terminal where they fuse with the neuronal plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Nfasc186 is highly mobile after insertion in the axonal membrane.
source: Nfasc186 is highly mobile after insertion in the axonal membrane and diffuses bidirectionally until immobilised at the AIS through its interaction with AnkyrinG.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FRAP and FLIP experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Nfasc186 diffuses bidirectionally in the axonal membrane until immobilised at the AIS through its interaction with AnkyrinG.
source: Nfasc186 is highly mobile after insertion in the axonal membrane and diffuses bidirectionally until immobilised at the AIS through its interaction with AnkyrinG.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FRAP-FLIP experiments and mutant analysis shown in Figures 3, 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Kv7.3 is similarly recruited to the AIS as Nfasc186.
source: Kv7.3 is similarly recruited to the AIS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The axon initial segment (AIS) is located at the proximal part of the axon.
source: The axon initial segment (AIS) is located at the proximal part of the axon where the high density of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) promotes the initiation and propagation of nerve impulses (Leterrier, 2018; Palay et al., 1968).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The high density of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) at the AIS promotes the initiation and propagation of nerve impulses.
source: The axon initial segment (AIS) is located at the proximal part of the axon where the high density of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) promotes the initiation and propagation of nerve impulses (Leterrier, 2018; Palay et al., 1968).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Changes in AIS size and length can influence neuronal excitability in the mature nervous system.
source: After AIS assembly during development, this domain can retain a degree of plasticity such that changes in its size and length can influence neuronal excitability in the mature nervous system (Grubb et al., 2011; Petersen et al., 2017; Kuba, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AIS morphological plasticity reflects the ability of the AIS to change the amount of its constituent proteins rather than their density.
source: This morphological plasticity reflects the ability of the AIS to change the amount of its constituent proteins rather than their density (Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of Nfasc186 in culture and in vivo causes the disintegration of the AIS with the loss of Nav, AnkG, βIV-Spectrin and Nr-CAM.
source: Deletion of Nfasc186 in culture and in vivo causes the disintegration of the AIS with the loss of Nav, AnkG, βIV-Spectrin and Nr-CAM; the consequent disordered electrophysiology impairs motor learning (Alpizar et al., 2019; Zonta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The consequent disordered electrophysiology from Nfasc186 deletion impairs motor learning.
source: Deletion of Nfasc186 in culture and in vivo causes the disintegration of the AIS with the loss of Nav, AnkG, βIV-Spectrin and Nr-CAM; the consequent disordered electrophysiology impairs motor learning (Alpizar et al., 2019; Zonta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Direct fusion of transport vesicles at the proximal axon does not contribute to the accumulation of Nfasc186 at the AIS.
source: Unlike Nav1.6, direct fusion of transport vesicles at the proximal axon does not contribute to the accumulation of Nfasc186 at the AIS (Akin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by FRAP-FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Interaction with AnkG immobilises Nfasc186 at the AIS but is unnecessary for the incorporation of the protein into the axonal membrane.
source: Interaction with AnkG immobilises Nfasc186 at the AIS but is unnecessary for the incorporation of the protein into the axonal membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with the AnkG binding mutant shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Kv7.3 interacts with AnkG.
source: Kv7.3 also interacts with AnkG (Pan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 1998) and follows a similar route to the AIS (Devaux et al., 2004; Pan et al., 2006; Rasmussen et al., 2007; Shah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Kv7.3 follows a similar route to the AIS as Nfasc186.
source: Kv7.3 also interacts with AnkG (Pan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 1998) and follows a similar route to the AIS (Devaux et al., 2004; Pan et al., 2006; Rasmussen et al., 2007; Shah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by both citations and experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nfasc186 is transported in vesicles generated in the secretory pathway by microtubule-based fast axonal transport.
source: Nfasc186 is transported in vesicles generated in the secretory pathway by microtubule-based fast axonal transport, which is probably Kinesin 1-dependent (Barry et al., 2014; Bekku and Salzer, 2020; Fréal et al., 2019 ; Ichinose et al., 2019; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nfasc186 transport is probably Kinesin 1-dependent.
source: Nfasc186 is transported in vesicles generated in the secretory pathway by microtubule-based fast axonal transport, which is probably Kinesin 1-dependent (Barry et al., 2014; Bekku and Salzer, 2020; Fréal et al., 2019 ; Ichinose et al., 2019; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents inference from previous studies.

claim: SEP is a pH-sensitive GFP-derivative that allows selective imaging of Nfasc186 expressed at the cell surface.
source: SEP is a pH-sensitive GFP-derivative that allows selective imaging of Nfasc186 expressed at the cell surface (Ashby et al., 2004; Ashby et al., 2006; Hildick et al., 2012; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Martin et al., 2008; Wilkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing SEP properties.

claim: Enrichment of SEP-Nfasc186 at the AIS relative to the soma or distal axon was not significantly different from that of endogenous neuronal Nfasc186, either on a wild type (WT) or a Neurofascin-null background.
source: Enrichment of the fusion protein at the AIS relative to the soma or distal axon was not significantly different from that of endogenous neuronal Nfasc186, either on a wild type (WT) or a Neurofascin-null background (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 was strongly expressed at the cell surface of the soma and axon terminal at DIV 3 prior to AIS formation.
source: Hence, neurons were transfected at DIV 2, and imaged the next day prior to AIS formation. SEP-Nfasc186 was strongly expressed at the cell surface of the soma and axon terminal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Coexpression of KHC560-halo confirmed the axon terminal as a primary location of SEP-Nfasc186 accumulation at the cell surface.
source: Coexpression of KHC560-halo confirmed the axon terminal as a primary location of SEP-Nfasc186 accumulation at the cell surface (Figure 1C; Twelvetrees et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C and a citation to the KHC560-halo marker.

claim: Fluorescence of SEP-Nfasc186 was readily detectable in the axonal membrane relative to background.
source: A line scan of SEP-Nfasc186 signal intensity at the cell soma, axon and axon terminal of the neuron in the upper panel of Figure 1C showed that fluorescence was readily detectable in the axonal membrane relative to background (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by line scan data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neither the absence of the over-expressed Kinesin nor reduced Nfasc186 expression on a Neurofascin-null background influenced the localisation of SEP-Nfasc186.
source: Neither the absence of the over-expressed Kinesin nor reduced Nfasc186 expression on a Neurofascin-null background influenced the localisation of SEP-Nfasc186 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Immunostaining using an antibody against an extracellular domain of the endogenous protein revealed Nfasc186 at the membrane surface of the soma and the axon terminus as found for SEP-Nfasc186.
source: and immunostaining using an antibody against an extracellular domain of the endogenous protein revealed Nfasc186 at the membrane surface of the soma and the axon terminus as found for SEP-Nfasc186 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 is a suitable proxy for assessing the localisation of endogenous neuronal Neurofascin.
source: We concluded that SEP-Nfasc186 is a suitable proxy for assessing the localisation of endogenous neuronal Neurofascin.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Live imaging revealed transient increases in the fluorescent intensity of SEP-Nfasc186 at the surface of the axon terminal suggesting possible exocytotic fusion events.
source: Live imaging revealed transient increases in the fluorescent intensity of SEP-Nfasc186 at the surface of the axon terminal suggesting possible exocytotic fusion events. (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2A and represents inference from the observed transient signals.

claim: TIRF analysis showed that surface delivery of SEP-Nfasc186 is particularly active at the cell body and axon terminus, but not at the axon itself.
source: TIRF analysis showed that surface delivery of SEP-Nfasc186 is particularly active at the cell body and axon terminus, but not at the axon itself (Figure 2B and C; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and C and Video 1.

claim: The periodic actin/spectrin axonal cytoskeleton may play a role in limiting exocytotic events in the axon.
source: The periodic actin/spectrin axonal cytoskeleton may play a role in limiting exocytotic events in the axon (Leterrier, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of SEP-Nfasc186 signal proximal to the ROI during FLIP indicated that SEP-Nfasc186 moves laterally in the axonal membrane from the axon terminus.
source: Loss of SEP-Nfasc186 signal proximal to the region of interest (ROI) indicated that SEP-Nfasc186 moves laterally in the axonal membrane from the axon terminus (Figure 3A–C; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP experimental data shown in Figure 3A–C and Video 2.

claim: Diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 in the axon membrane is bidirectional and can also occur anterogradely.
source: Furthermore, since FLIP does not bleach vesicular SEP-Nfasc186, the loss of signal intensity at the axon terminal apparent in Figure 3A shows that diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 in the axon membrane is bidirectional and can also occur anterogradely, as confirmed by asymmetric FLIP at the AIS with reference to Figure 4 (see below).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP data shown in Figure 3A and asymmetric FLIP experiments referenced in the text.

claim: Nocodazole strongly inhibited vesicular transport of Nfasc186-Dendra2.
source: This is also evident for vesicles transporting Nfasc186-Dendra2 and kymographic analysis of their movement immediately proximal to the axon terminal showed that although nocodazole strongly inhibited vesicular transport of Nfasc186-Dendra2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is supported by kymographic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Nocodazole had no effect on the retrograde movement of photoconverted Nfasc186-Dendra2.
source: kymographic analysis of their movement immediately proximal to the axon terminal showed that although nocodazole strongly inhibited vesicular transport of Nfasc186-Dendra2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), it had no effect on the retrograde movement of photoconverted Nfasc186-Dendra2 (Figure 3D and E; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 3D and E and Video 3.

claim: The signal arising from the retrograde movement of photoconverted Nfasc186-Dendra2 visualised in the axon primarily reflects fluorescence from cell surface protein.
source: Hence, the signal arising from the retrograde movement of photoconverted Nfasc186-Dendra2 visualised in the axon primarily reflects fluorescence from cell surface protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nocodazole experiment results showing that vesicular transport is blocked but membrane diffusion continues.

claim: Nfasc186 is extremely mobile after insertion in the neuronal membrane and can move towards the AIS in the plane of the axonal membrane.
source: In summary, Nfasc186 is extremely mobile after insertion in the neuronal membrane and can move towards the AIS in the plane of the axonal membrane.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the FLIP and photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: SEP-Kv7.3 shows a similar pattern of enrichment and delivery to the neuronal membrane at the cell body and axon terminus before the formation of the AIS.
source: The fusion protein SEP-Kv7.3 shows a similar pattern of enrichment and delivery to the neuronal membrane at the cell body and axon terminus before the formation of the AIS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: FLIP at the axon immediately proximal to the axon terminal showed that Kv7.3 also undergoes retrograde movement from the axon terminus in the axonal membrane.
source: Furthermore, FLIP at the axon immediately proximal to the axon terminal showed that Kv7.3 also undergoes retrograde movement from the axon terminus in the axonal membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 was highly mobile in the distal axonal membrane.
source: FRAP showed not only that SEP-Nfasc186 was highly mobile in the distal axonal membrane but also that its mobility was unaffected by either the inhibition of myosin II ATPase activity with Blebbistatin or disruption of microfilaments with latrunculin A (Figure 4A and B; Berger et al., 2018; Sobotzik et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in the distal axonal membrane was unaffected by either the inhibition of myosin II ATPase activity with Blebbistatin or disruption of microfilaments with latrunculin A.
source: FRAP showed not only that SEP-Nfasc186 was highly mobile in the distal axonal membrane but also that its mobility was unaffected by either the inhibition of myosin II ATPase activity with Blebbistatin or disruption of microfilaments with latrunculin A (Figure 4A and B; Berger et al., 2018; Sobotzik et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data with drug treatments shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Nfasc186 can diffuse from the somatic or axon terminal plasma membrane to the AIS unassisted by the underlying cytoskeleton or its associated motor proteins.
source: Hence, Nfasc186 can diffuse from the somatic or axon terminal plasma membrane to the AIS unassisted by the underlying cytoskeleton or its associated motor proteins (see also Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the drug treatment experiments and photoconversion data.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for Nfasc186 in the distal axon is 0.37 ± 0.01 µm2/s.
source: The diffusion coefficient for Nfasc186 in the distal axon is 0.37 ± 0.01 µm2/s and is comparable to the previously reported value for highly mobile, untethered axonal Nfasc186 (0.34 ± 0.02 µm2/s) (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FRAP data analysis.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for Nfasc186 in the distal axon is comparable to the previously reported value for highly mobile, untethered axonal Nfasc186 (0.34 ± 0.02 µm2/s).
source: The diffusion coefficient for Nfasc186 in the distal axon is 0.37 ± 0.01 µm2/s and is comparable to the previously reported value for highly mobile, untethered axonal Nfasc186 (0.34 ± 0.02 µm2/s) (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: Maturation of the AIS was accompanied by a significant reduction in the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 (recovery 46.1 ± 0.8% at DIV 5-6 and 34.3 ± 1.6% at DIV 12-13).
source: Maturation of the AIS was accompanied by a significant reduction in the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 (recovery 46.1 ± 0.8% and 34.3 ± 1.6%, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data comparing different time points shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Accumulation of SEP-Nfasc186 at the soma and axon terminal continued during AIS assembly.
source: Accumulation of SEP-Nfasc186 at the soma and axon terminal continued during AIS assembly (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FRAP revealed substantial recovery of fluorescence within the AIS.
source: FRAP revealed substantial recovery of fluorescence within the AIS: however, this recovery is abolished by FLIP (Figure 4E and F; Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4E and F and Video 5.

claim: Fluorescence recovery at the AIS after FRAP is abolished by FLIP.
source: FRAP revealed substantial recovery of fluorescence within the AIS: however, this recovery is abolished by FLIP (Figure 4E and F; Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP-FLIP data shown in Figure 4E and F and Video 5.

claim: Recovery of fluorescence at the AIS is due to lateral movement of SEP-Nfasc186 in the axonal membrane with no significant contribution from direct vesicular fusion.
source: We concluded that recovery of fluorescence is due to lateral movement of SEP-Nfasc186 in the axonal membrane with no significant contribution from direct vesicular fusion.
evidence: This conclusion is based on FRAP-FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 into the AIS was bidirectional (recovery: 13.2 ± 0.2%-distal FLIP; 11.9 ± 0.7%-proximal FLIP).
source: By performing asymmetric FLIP on just one side of the ROI instead of bilaterally we were able to show that lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 into the AIS was bidirectional (recovery: 13.2 ± 0.2%-distal FLIP; 11.9 ± 0.7%-proximal FLIP; mean ± SEM, n = 3, Student's t test, not significant).
evidence: This is supported by asymmetric FLIP experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Fusion of Nfasc186 transport vesicles and concomitant protein insertion at the AIS itself is not a substantial source of surface-expressed AIS Nfasc186 in cortical neurons.
source: We conclude that fusion of Nfasc186 transport vesicles and concomitant protein insertion at the AIS itself is not a substantial source of surface-expressed AIS Nfasc186 in cortical neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is based on FRAP-FLIP experiments showing no recovery when lateral diffusion is blocked.

claim: Bidirectional lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane is the dominant mechanism by which Nfasc186 enters the AIS.
source: In contrast, bidirectional lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane is the dominant mechanism by which Nfasc186 enters the AIS.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the FRAP-FLIP experiments and asymmetric FLIP data.

claim: Intra-axonal vesicular SEP-Nfasc186 is neither fluorescent nor susceptible to photobleaching.
source: Nevertheless, we wished to confirm that SEP does indeed report Nfasc186 exclusively at the neuronal surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), and, using a refined protocol, we confirmed that intra-axonal vesicular SEP-Nfasc186 is neither fluorescent nor susceptible to photobleaching (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fluorescence recovery at the Purkinje cell AIS was by lateral diffusion in the plane of the axonal membrane, as found for cortical neurons.
source: FRAP-FLIP analysis of acute cerebellar slices from P10 transgenic mice showed that fluorescence recovery at the Purkinje cell AIS was indeed by lateral diffusion in the plane of the axonal membrane, as found for cortical neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP-FLIP data from cerebellar slices shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: AnkG is believed to act as a pioneer constituent and key organizer of the nascent AIS.
source: AnkG is believed to act as a pioneer constituent and key organizer of the nascent AIS (Dzhashiashvili et al., 2007; Galiano et al., 2012; Hedstrom et al., 2008; Jenkins and Bennett, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutation of the AnkG binding site prevents SEP-Nfasc186YA accumulation at the AIS.
source: Numerous studies have emphasized the importance of the interaction of Nfasc186 with AnkG at the AIS and we confirmed that mutation of the AnkG binding site prevents SEP-Nfasc186YA accumulation at the AIS (Boiko et al., 2007; Davis and Bennett, 1994; Fréal et al., 2019; Lemaillet et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 1998; Zonta et al., 2011; Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with the mutant shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–C and citations.

claim: FRAP confirmed that the mutant protein SEP-Nfasc186YA was highly mobile at the AIS of cortical neurons.
source: FRAP confirmed that the mutant protein was indeed highly mobile at the AIS of cortical neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5D–F.

claim: The accumulation and insertion of Nfasc186 at the surface membrane of the axon terminal does not require interaction with AnkG.
source: Nevertheless, the accumulation and insertion of Nfasc186 at the surface membrane of the axon terminal does not require interaction with AnkG (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data of the mutant at the axon terminal shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G.

claim: Neither the insertion of Nfasc186 into the neuronal membrane nor its mobility in the axonal membrane requires the cotransport of an AnkG/AIS membrane protein complex.
source: Hence, neither the insertion of Nfasc186 into the neuronal membrane nor its mobility in the axonal membrane requires the cotransport of an AnkG/AIS membrane protein complex.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mutant experiments showing normal delivery and mobility without AnkG binding.

claim: The AnkG binding mutant of Nfasc186 retained high mobility (recovery 78.6 ± 2.0% at DIV 5-6 and 79.1 ± 1.5% at DIV 12-13) during the same period when wild-type Nfasc186 became more immobilized.
source: Further, although the fractional recovery of SEP-Nfasc186 at the AIS declined between 5–6 and 12–13 days in culture (Figure 4D), the AnkG binding mutant of Nfasc186 retained high mobility (recovery 78.6 ± 2.0% and 79.1 ± 1.5%, respectively) during the same period (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data comparing wild-type and mutant over time shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–F.

claim: As Nfasc186 becomes increasingly immobilised during the early stages of AIS formation, it is the interaction of Nfasc186 with AnkG that is overwhelmingly important in anchoring and immobilizing Neurofascin at the surface of the AIS.
source: This shows that as Nfasc186 becomes increasingly immobilised during the early stages of AIS formation (Figure 4C), it is the interaction of Nfasc186 with AnkG that is overwhelmingly important in anchoring and immobilizing Neurofascin at the surface of the AIS.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparing wild-type and mutant mobility data over time.

claim: Vesicles that transport Nfasc186 are able to fuse with the somatic plasma membrane and distally to the axon terminal membrane, but they do not insert Nfasc186 at the AIS directly.
source: Our model indicates that vesicles that transport Nfasc186 are able to fuse not only with the somatic plasma membrane but also distally to the axon terminal membrane, but they do not insert Nfasc186 at the AIS directly.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings based on all the experimental data.

claim: This model of sequential membrane delivery and clustering may also inform studies on how transmembrane proteins are recruited to the node of Ranvier in myelinated axons.
source: Since Nfasc186 has a major role in assembling the node of Ranvier in myelinated axons, this model of sequential membrane delivery and clustering may also inform studies on how transmembrane proteins are recruited to the node (Davis et al., 1996; Sherman et al., 2005; Tait et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2012; Zonta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about broader implications supported by citations.

claim: Nfasc186 has a major role in assembling the node of Ranvier in myelinated axons.
source: Since Nfasc186 has a major role in assembling the node of Ranvier in myelinated axons, this model of sequential membrane delivery and clustering may also inform studies on how transmembrane proteins are recruited to the node (Davis et al., 1996; Sherman et al., 2005; Tait et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2012; Zonta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The anterograde velocity of vesicles transporting Nfasc186-mCh was 2.3 ± 0.27 μm/s.
source: Kymograph analysis of 5 axons showed that the anterograde velocity was 2.3 ± 0.27 μm/s and retrograde velocity was 1.9 ± 0.18 μm/s (mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from kymograph analysis shown in Video 4.

claim: The retrograde velocity of vesicles transporting Nfasc186-mCh was 1.9 ± 0.18 μm/s.
source: Kymograph analysis of 5 axons showed that the anterograde velocity was 2.3 ± 0.27 μm/s and retrograde velocity was 1.9 ± 0.18 μm/s (mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from kymograph analysis shown in Video 4.
